activity: Rose is watching a big game with family and friends.
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Rose went to the big game with Dad and Gran. The field was wide and green. There were one, two, three balls by the fence. There were lots and lots of people. "Can I see the game?" Rose asked. "Not yet," said Gran. The people in front were very tall.

Rose tried to peek between the tall people. She saw a shoe. She saw a red shirt. She did not see the ball. "What will help me see?" she asked. "Ask Dad," said Gran. "Dad, can you lift me up?" said Rose. Dad picked her up, up, up.

Now Rose could see the whole field. She saw the red shirt kick the ball. Then the ball went into the net. All the people shouted, "Good goal!" Rose clapped her hands. Then everyone sat down. Rose sat down too. She saw one shoe again.

Rose stood up. Then she saw the whole field again. Sit down, see one shoe. Stand up, see the ball. "I can see the game my own way," said Rose. Dad took out his phone. "Say cheese," he said. Rose stood up tall. "Cheese!" she said. Click went the phone.

activity: Through what Mateo sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules.
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Mateo ran to the swings at the park. There were only two swings. A girl was on one swing already. Mateo wanted the other swing.

A big boy pushed past him. The big boy got on the swing first. Mateo stopped and waited. He did not push. He watched the swing go up and down. "Can I have a turn next?" Mateo asked. The big boy nodded.

The sun made the girl's swing slow down. "My turn," she said, and she hopped off. She did not have to wait long, because the big boy counted to twenty out loud. Then he jumped off too. "Your turn," he said.

Mateo got on the swing. He pumped his legs hard. The swing went high. His shadow stretched dark and long on the ground. A small boy came to wait. "You can go next," Mateo said. "I will count to twenty, like him." He counted slow. Waiting gave the small boy a turn, and gave Mateo a friend to chase after. "Catch me!" the small boy yelled, and they ran.

activity: Jade is learning something new. What Jade is learning: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing.
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Jade went to Milo's house. Milo had a new toy dinosaur. It was green and it could roar.

"Can I hold it?" asked Jade.

"You can have a turn after me," said Milo.

Jade wanted the dinosaur now. She reached out her hand. She almost grabbed it.

Then she stopped. She sat on her hands. They felt warm under her legs.

Milo made the dinosaur stomp near her shoe. "Roar!" he said. "The dinosaur wants cookies." Jade laughed.

"Okay," said Milo. "Your turn now." He put the dinosaur in her hands. It was a little heavy. Jade made it hop on the couch.

Milo sat and waited. He did not grab. He watched the dinosaur hop.

Then something silly happened. Jade pressed the dinosaur's tummy. The dinosaur burped instead of roaring!

Milo fell over laughing. "Do it again!" he said.

Jade pressed the tummy again. Burp!

"Now my turn," said Milo. He held out his hands.

Jade gave him the dinosaur. He made it roar and burp and roar again.

"Best dinosaur ever," said Jade.

"My mom bought it with birthday money," said Milo. "Want a snack?"

They filled a bowl with crackers and shared that too.

activity: Charlotte is learning something new. What Charlotte is learning: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes.
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Charlotte sat on the little red chair in the school library. She wanted a book about a boot. She could not find it anywhere.

Her friend Sam came by. "Are you sad?" he asked.

"I want the boot book," said Charlotte. "But I can't read the letters yet."

Sam picked up a book. He pointed to the first letter. "That is B," he said. "B says buh."

Charlotte looked at the letter B. Then she said the word boot out loud. "Buh. Boot!" The book in her hand had a bear on it. "Bear starts with buh too!" She put that one back.

She ran her finger along the shelf. B. B. B. Here was one with a boot on the cover! Charlotte opened it up on her lap.

Sam bumped the table and his juice began to spill. Charlotte grabbed the book and held it high, safe and dry.

"Thanks," said Sam.

"Letters talk," said Charlotte. "B says buh. That is how I found it."

activity: Arthur is searching for a lost favorite toy.
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Arthur held his little blue dog at the grocery store. The dog had a spot of white paint on its ear. Arthur put the dog in the cart seat. Then he ran to see the apples.

When he came back, the dog was gone. Arthur looked under the cart. No dog. He looked by the bread. No dog.

A big dog walked by. It went, "Bark! Bark!" Then the big dog sniffed at a shelf. It sniffed and sniffed. Something fell down with a soft bump. It was the little blue dog!

Arthur picked it up and hugged it tight. "Good dog," he said. "You found him first." The big dog wagged its tail. Arthur climbed back into the cart with his dog and smiled all the way home.

activity: Through what Felix sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green.
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Felix went to the store with Mom. He wanted a sweet apple for snack. He saw apples in a big bin. Some were red. Some were green. Some were yellow.

"I want a green one," said Felix. Green was his favorite color. He picked a green apple. He held it up high.

Mom leaned close to him. "The red ones are sweet," she whispered. "The green ones taste sour." Felix did not change his mind. He put the green apple in the basket.

At home, Felix took a big bite. His mouth made a funny face. The apple was sour! "I picked the wrong apple," he said. He looked at his mom. "The green apple is sour because green apples are sour ones." Mom nodded and smiled. She cut a red apple for him. Felix took a bite. It was sweet like juice. It was the best apple ever.

At the store, Felix had seen a little green bug on the lettuce. Now he thought about the bug. "The bug likes green things," he whispered. "But I like red apples best." He gave Mom a big hug and took another sweet, red bite.

activity: Through what Asher sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them.
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Asher ran to the backyard with his red bucket. He wanted to fill it with sand. He wore his warm hat and coat.

The wind began to blow. It blew his hat right off his head. The hat rolled across the grass. Asher chased it. The wind pushed it under the bush. Asher pulled, but the hat was stuck. Then the wind stopped. The hat sat still. Asher picked it up. "The wind made my hat go," he said. "The wind stopped, so my hat stopped too."

Next, the sun came out. It was sunny and warm. Asher took off his coat. He filled his bucket with sand. Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Big drops hit his shirt. Soon his shirt was wet. "Rain makes my clothes wet," said Asher. "Sunny is warm, but rainy is wet." He held his hat over the sand so it would stay dry.

Asher ran inside to Mom. She helped him into a dry shirt and rain boots. "In snow, you wear warm boots too," said Mom. Asher smiled. "Maybe we can play in snow next!" He set his bucket by the door, all ready.

activity: Through what Iris sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Iris sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread. It sat far away by Dad.

She reached and reached. Her arm was too short. She reached more. Her glass tipped. Water ran across the table like a little river.

"Oh no," said Iris. "Sorry, Mama."

"That is okay," said Mama. Iris helped wipe the water with a towel. The towel got wet and heavy. Mama wrung it out for her.

Then Iris sat still. She looked at the bread. She looked at Dad.

"Please pass the bread, Dad," she said.

Dad smiled. He passed the basket. Iris took a warm roll.

"Thank you, Dad," she said.

"Can you help me, Mama?" Iris asked. "The butter is too hard."

"Of course," said Mama. She cut a small piece. Iris spread it slowly. Some butter fell on the table. Iris did not reach. She froze and put her hands in her lap.

"Please, may I have the towel?" she asked.

Mama handed it over. "Nice asking," she said.

Iris wiped the spot all by herself. The table was clean again. She took a big bite of her roll.

"This is the best bread ever," said Iris. "Thank you for making it, Dad."

Dad cut her one more roll, warm and soft.

activity: Luna is learning something new. What Luna is learning: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal.
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Luna held her grandma's hand at the festival. Big tents stood in a row. Something warm and sweet filled the air. "I'm hungry," Luna said.

Grandma smiled. "Soon we will eat with everyone. But first, we say our blessing together."

Long tables sat under a low tent. People carried bread and soup and rice. Grandma helped set out the bowls. Luna used a spoon to dig rice from a big pot into a bowl. One scoop, then another. Soon every bowl was full.

Then everyone went quiet. They held hands. Grandma held Luna's hand on one side. A boy held her other side. His hand was small, like hers.

"Bless this food and bless us all," the people said together. Luna said it too, quiet at first, then loud. After the blessing, everyone began to eat. The boy passed Luna the bread before he took his own slice. Grandma poured tea for the neighbor across the table.

A small feather floated down and landed near Luna's plate. She picked it up and put it in her pocket. Then she took a big bite of warm bread.

"This is the best festival," she said.

activity: Through what Julia sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that plants and animals need food, water and a place to live.
knowledge_domain: the idea that plants and animals need food, water and a place to live
story:
Julia looked for her cat, Milo. He was not on the porch. He was not in the grass. She found him under the curly leaves of the big pumpkin plant.

"Why are you here, Milo?" she asked. Milo was drinking from a little puddle. He was eating his food bowl... no, that was empty. "You are hungry and thirsty!" Julia said. She filled his bowl with water. She gave him his food. Milo ate and drank. Then he went back under the leaves. "Why do you stay there?" she asked. "Because it is your house!"

Julia looked at the pumpkin plant. It had water from the rain. It had food from the soil. It had a home in the warm sun. "You need water, food and a home," she said. "Just like Milo. Just like me!"

Julia helped by giving the plant a drink from her small can. She put a worm near its roots. "There," she said. "Now you have a snack, too." Milo purred under the curly leaves, and Julia sat down beside him.

activity: Through what Amira sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green.
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Amira was at Grandma's house. She wanted to paint a picture of a tree. Grandma got out the paints and small cups of water.

"Grandma, I need green paint," said Amira. "The leaves are green." Grandma looked in the box. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was no green. "Oh no," said Amira. Her tummy felt tight like a fist.

"Let's try something," said Grandma. She put a blob of yellow on the plate. Then she put a blob of blue next to it. "Stir them with your brush," she said. Amira stirred round and round. The brush made a swoosh sound. The yellow turned softer. Then it turned darker. Then it turned green!

"Grandma! Yellow and blue make green!" said Amira. She said it again, so she would not forget. "Yellow and blue make green." Grandma laughed and clapped her hands.

Amira painted a big green tree. She painted a red bird and a blue sky. Then she painted yellow flowers under the tree. When the paint was dry, Grandma put glue on the back of the paper. They stuck it on the fridge. Amira stood back and looked. "Yellow and blue make green," she told the red bird.

activity: Through what Milo sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow.
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Milo ran to the park with his dad. The sun was hot on his face. He sat in the shade and it felt cold there. "It is cool under the tree," he said.

Milo wanted to play with the big red ball. But a big dog ran fast and knocked it away. The ball rolled under a bench. A tiny ant walked slow on the ground. Milo watched it crawl up a rough stick.

"The ball is stuck," said Milo. Dad had an idea. He took off his jacket and covered his hand. He reached under the bench. Out came a big red ball, and one small blue marble too. "Look, a marble!" said Milo.

Milo held the marble up to the sun. It made a small bright spot on the ground. He moved his hand and the spot moved too. "It follows me!" he said. Dad laughed. Then they walked home, the big ball under Milo's arm and the small marble in his pocket. "Again tomorrow?" asked Milo. "Again tomorrow," said Dad.

activity: Nolan is learning something new. What Nolan is learning: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done.
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Nolan sat on the rug at Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. Nolan wanted to draw a big red truck on it. But the screen was dark.

"It sleeps like a cat," said Mia. "Watch this." She pushed the little round button. The screen lit up. It looked bright and smooth. Nolan laughed. "It woke up!"

"Your turn," said Mia. Nolan pushed the button too. The screen went dark again. He pushed it once more. The screen lit up. Push, dark. Push, light. "You are a magic button," Nolan told it.

"Now tap the blue crayon picture," said Mia. Nolan tapped it with one finger. The drawing page opened. He drew a red truck. He drew one wheel like a sock, big and floppy. Mia giggled. "Trucks don't wear socks!" So Nolan drew a round wheel instead.

Then the doorbell rang. Snack time. "We put the tablet away now," said Mia. She laid it flat in the basket. Nolan helped push it in, gentle like tucking in a baby. "Night night, truck," he said.

"Good night, sock wheel," said Mia.

Cookies were waiting on the table. Nolan took a big bite. "Best button ever," he said.

activity: Hunter is learning something new. What Hunter is learning: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling.
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Hunter wanted to make his own breakfast. He got the bread and the butter. He tried to spread the butter. He pushed too hard. The bread tore into two pieces.

He tried again with new bread. This time he made soft, little strokes. The butter went on slow and smooth. The bread stayed whole.

Then he got the milk. He held the pitcher up high. The milk made a loud glug. It splashed over the cup and onto the table.

Hunter looked at the puddle. He got a cloth and wiped it up. Then he sat the cup on the table. He put the pitcher spout close to the cup. He tipped it just a little. The milk slid in quiet and slow. Not one drop spilled.

Hunter took a bite of toast. A bit of butter sat on his lip. He licked it off with his tongue.

"When the milk pours from way up high, it goes everywhere," he said. "When it pours from close, it goes in the cup."

He drank all his milk down.

activity: Through what Dylan sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed.
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Dylan sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a big growl. "I want noodles," he said.

Mom put the pot on the stove. She stirred and stirred. Dylan waited. He looked at his fork. He looked at his cup. He waited some more.

At last Mom brought the bowl. Dylan ate one bite. Then he ate more. His tummy felt warm and happy.

Then Dylan spilled some water on his shirt. His sleeve was wet. "Oh no," he said.

"That's okay," said Dad. "After dinner, you can have a bath. Then you put on a dry shirt. Then it is bed time."

Dylan ate his last noodle. He carried his cup to the sink, slow and careful. No water fell.

"Good job," said Dad. Dylan smiled.

Bath time came next. The water was warm. Dad washed Dylan's hair. Dylan splashed a little. Then Dad helped him dry off with a big towel.

Dylan put on his dry pajamas. The shirt was soft and warm.

"One story," said Mom. "Then sleep."

Dylan picked a book about a bear. Mom read it. Dylan yawned. He closed his eyes.

"Good night, Dylan," Mom whispered. She turned off the light.

activity: Mya is learning something new. What Mya is learning: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour.
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Mya wanted to paint a flower for Dad. She had red paint, yellow paint, and blue paint. "Red, yellow, blue," she said. She said it again. "Red, yellow, blue." Three cups. Three colours.

But Dad's favourite flower was purple. Mya had no purple paint. She looked and looked. No purple cup anywhere. Her shoulders went down low.

Then she had an idea. She dipped her brush in red. She dipped it in blue too. She swirled them together in a big spot. The spot turned purple! Mya hopped up and down. "Red and blue make purple!" she said.

She painted a big purple flower. When night came, she set it by the door. In the morning, Dad would find it. Mya smiled and whispered, "Purple for Dad."

activity: Mia is making an art or craft project.
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Mia sat at the big table. She had paper and glue. She wanted to make a wild lion picture. Outside, the rain went tap, tap, tap on the window.

Mia spread glue on the paper with her brush. She stirred the glue pot with a stick, round and round. Then she poured on yellow paper strips for the lion's mane. But the strips fell off. They slid down to the table. Mia frowned.

Then she saw the glue on the paper was still wet and shiny. The strips stuck where the glue was wet. Where it was dry, they fell. "Oh!" said Mia. "The wet glue holds them. Dry spots let go." So she brushed more glue on each dry spot. She pressed the strips down with her hands.

Mama came over with a towel. "Your hands are sticky," said Mama. "Let me help." Mama wiped Mia's fingers, one by one. Mia held up the lion. Its mane was big and wild. "Look, Mama! The glue is drying. The lion stays on!" said Mia. The rain kept tapping, and the lion dried by the window.

activity: Through what Sarah sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle.
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Sarah wanted to make a picture for Mama. She had paper and crayons on the table. But what should she draw?

She looked around the room. The clock on the wall was round like a circle. "One circle," she said. The window had four sides, all the same. "One square." The slice of toast on her plate had three pointy corners. "One triangle." The door was tall with two long sides. "One rectangle."

Sarah drew them all. A circle, a square, a triangle, a rectangle. Then she held her paper up next to the lamp. A big shadow fell on the wall. "Look, Mama! My shapes made more shapes!"

Mama smiled and pinned the picture up. "Let me count them," she said. "One, two, three, four shapes."

"Four shapes," said Sarah, "and four shadows too."

activity: Through what Mason sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle.
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Mason ran to the library with Dad. He wanted the truck book. But the truck book was gone. "We can lose a book spot," said the librarian. "Let's hunt for it!"

Mason looked at the big rug. He saw circles on it. Round circles, like his plate at home. He jumped on one. It felt soft under his shoes.

Then he saw square tiles on the floor. Four sides, all the same. He stepped from square to square. Clap, clap, clap went his shoes.

Next to the shelf, he saw a triangle sign. It had three pointy corners. It pointed up high. Mason looked up. There was the truck book on the top shelf!

Dad reached up and got it. The book was warm from the sunny window. It was shaped like a rectangle, long and flat.

At lunch, Mason ate his sandwich and told Dad, "The rug circles helped me find it!" He took a big, happy bite.

activity: Through what Logan sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them.
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Logan waited at the bus stop with Mama. He wanted to wear his new hat. But which day was a hat day?

The sun came out. It was sunny. Logan felt warm on his nose. He did not need the hat yet. He took off one shoe and wiggled his toe in the air.

Then the wind blew. It was windy. Leaves began to roll down the street. Logan's hair flew up. He put the hat on. The wind could not blow it away now. "Good thinking," said Mama.

Little drops fell. It was rainy. Mama opened a big umbrella over them. Logan held it with one toe touching the pole, helping.

The rain turned white and soft. It was snowy. Snow sat on Logan's hat. It sat on his toe of his boot, too.

The bus came. Logan climbed up with Mama. His hat was warm and dry. "Bus!" he said, and off they went.

activity: Through what Connor sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited.
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Connor was in his bedroom. He wanted to paint a picture of the park. He got his paper and his paints. He was excited to start.

Connor made a big sun. Then his cup tipped over. Water ran across the paper. The sun got wet and turned into a blurry blob. Connor felt angry. "Oh no," he said. "My sun is gone!" He wanted to cry. He felt sad.

Mama came in. "What happened?" she asked. "My water spilled. Is my painting done for?" said Connor. Mama shook her head. "Let's wait," she said. "The paper has to dry." They waited and waited. Connor looked out the window. At last the paper was dry. Connor painted a new sun, right on top of the blob. Now it looked like a bright yellow flower. "Look, Mama! The spill made a flower!" said Connor. He felt happy again.

activity: Through what Blake sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules.
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Blake wanted to play with the round red ball. Her friend Sam held the ball in his hands.

"Can I have it?" asked Blake.

Sam shook his head. "It is mine," he said.

Blake looked at the toy bus on the rug. She picked up the bus. "You can have this," she said.

Sam put down the ball. He took the bus. He rolled it across the rug.

Blake held the ball now. She rolled it to Sam. Sam rolled it back.

"Now you," said Blake. She pushed the bus to Sam. Sam pushed it back to her.

Then Mia came in. She wanted to play too. Blake looked at the ball. She looked at the bus. She looked at Mia.

Blake rolled the ball to Mia. "Your turn," she said.

Mia smiled and rolled it back. They all sat in a circle on the rug. The ball went round and round, from Blake to Sam to Mia.

Teacher Kim clapped her hands softly. "Time to clean up," she said. Blake put the ball in the basket. Sam parked the bus by the shelf. Mia put the blocks away.

Then they all sat together for snack time.

activity: Eleanor is learning something new. What Eleanor is learning: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling.
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Eleanor woke up hungry. She wanted toast with butter. She wanted milk in her cup, too.

Dad put the toast on her plate. The butter sat in a little dish. Eleanor picked up her spoon. She pressed too hard. The toast tore into two pieces.

"Oops," said Eleanor.

"Try again," said Dad. He gave her a new slice.

This time Eleanor touched the butter lightly. The butter made a soft line on the toast. She moved the spoon slow and easy. The butter spread all over. It looked shiny and smooth.

Then Dad poured the milk. A little drop ran down the cup. Eleanor wiped it with her cloth. The puddle went away. She put the cup down and looked at her toast.

Dad smiled. "You did it yourself."

Eleanor took a big bite. "This is the best toast," she said. The milk did not spill. Not even one drop. She held her cup up high.

"Look, Dad!"

activity: Florence is learning something new. What Florence is learning: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands.
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Florence stood on the baseball diamond. She held a small red beanbag. Dad held up a big hoop.

"Throw it in," said Dad.

Florence threw the beanbag. It went low. It hit the dirt. She frowned and picked it up.

Then Dad rolled a big ball to her. She tried to catch it with one arm. The ball bounced off her elbow and rolled away.

Florence sat down on the bench. She picked up a stick and drew a circle in the dirt. What made the ball get away? What made the beanbag fall low?

She looked at her hands. One hand was little. Two hands were big, like a bowl. Maybe two hands could hold a big ball.

Dad rolled the ball again. Florence put both hands out. The ball landed in her two hands. She held it tight. "I caught it!" she said.

Then she lifted the beanbag up high, near her ear, and tossed it. Up it went, and down it dropped. It fell right into the hoop.

"Two hands catch the ball," said Florence. "And up high makes the beanbag go in!"

She ate a salty pretzel. Then she danced around the bases, holding her beanbag high.

activity: Axel is planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow.
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Axel stood on the balcony with his teacher. They had little pots and tiny seeds. "Seeds sleep in the dirt," said Axel. He patted the soil soft and flat. Every morning he looked. No green. No leaves. Axel was mad. He stomped his small foot. "Wake up, seeds! Wake up!"

Then his teacher gave him a small blue cup. "The seeds are thirsty," she said. Axel poured the water. Drip, drip, drip. He watered them every day. He touched the wet dirt with one finger. It felt cool.

One morning, Axel saw a green tip. Then two small leaves. "The water woke them up!" said Axel. He jumped up and down. The seeds did not sleep anymore. Axel held his cup and smiled. "More water, little plant. Grow, grow, grow."

activity: Xavier is learning to swim at the local pool.
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Xavier went to the big pool. His mom held his hands. "Kick your legs," she said. Xavier kicked. Splash, splash, splash.

Xavier wanted to reach the red ball. It was far away. He kicked and kicked. His legs made the water go fast. The water pushed him forward. "The kicking makes me go!" he said. His mom smiled and let go of one hand.

Xavier kicked some more. Kick, kick, kick. He got closer to the ball. Then his hand touched it. "I got it!" he said. His mom clapped. A girl next to them was holding the wall. She looked a little scared. Xavier pushed the red ball to her. "You can kick too," he said. "It makes you go quick."

The girl kicked one foot. Then two feet. She moved away from the wall a little bit. She laughed. "See?" said Xavier. "You live in the water now, like a little fish." He held her hand and they kicked together. Splash, splash, splash.

activity: Ibrahim is learning something new. What Ibrahim is learning: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more.
fact: When you count a group of things, the last number you say tells how many there are. You get the same answer no matter which one you count first.
story:
Ibrahim stood in Grandma's kitchen. Ten cookies sat on a flat tray. "Can I have one?" he asked. "First let's count them," said Grandma. "We need some for after dinner."

Ibrahim touched each cookie. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." "Very good," said Grandma. Ibrahim reached for a cookie. Then he stopped. "Wait," he said. "Let me count again." He started from the other end of the tray. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." He jumped up and down. "It is still ten!"

Grandpa came in with two bowls of grapes. "Which bowl has more?" he asked. Ibrahim counted the red bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Then he counted the green bowl. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." "The green one has more," said Ibrahim. "Seven is more than six." Grandpa tipped the green bowl toward him. "Then you may eat the extra one."

Ibrahim ate his grape. It had a seed inside, a tiny brown seed shaped like a little star. "Look, Grandma!" he cried. "A surprise in my grape!"

activity: Through what Elias sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Elias went to the park with his red ball. He threw it high. The ball did not come back. Where did it go?

Elias looked with his eyes. He saw tall grass. He listened with his ears. He heard no bounce at all. "Hmm," said Elias. "Can my ears find the ball? No, not with that part!"

He sniffed with his nose. The grass smelled green and fresh. But no ball smell. "Not with that part either!"

Then he put his hands over his ears. The birds went quiet. He took his hands off. The birds sang loud again. "My ears hear because they are open!" said Elias.

So he opened his eyes very wide. He walked into the tall grass. He touched with his fingers, left and right. His fingers touched something round and smooth. The ball!

He picked it up. "My eyes and my hands are a team," said Elias. He licked his lips. His snack was waiting. It would taste sweet, like strawberries. Elias ran to the wooden bench.

activity: Jacob is getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office.
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Jacob sat in the car. Mom turned the car into the parking lot. "We go to the doctor today," said Mom. "You get a little shot."

Jacob held his toy flower in his lap. The flower had soft pink petals. "Will it hurt?" he asked. "Just a tiny poke," said Mom.

At the doctor's office, a nurse said, "Can you hold your arm still?" Jacob squeezed his arm tight. He made it hard as a rock. The nurse touched his arm. "Oh, this arm is tight," she said. "Let us make it soft like your pillow." Jacob let his arm go soft and loose.

The nurse counted, "One, two, three." Quick poke. It was done! "That was little," said Jacob. He looked at his arm. He saw one small bandaid. "My arm was tight, and tight arms hurt more," Jacob said. "Soft arms are better." Mom smiled. The doctor gave Jacob a sticker shaped like a star.

In the car, the sun felt hot on his knees. Jacob held up his sticker. "Look, flower," he said, and put the star next to his pink toy flower.

activity: Nathan is losing a first wobbly tooth.
knowledge_domain: losing a first wobbly tooth
story:
Nathan sat at the dinner table. He had carrots on his plate. One carrot was bright orange. He took a big bite. Then something felt odd. His tooth moved! "Mom! My tooth wiggles!" he said. Mom smiled. Dad leaned close to look.

Nathan wiggled the tooth with his tongue. It went back and forth. He wanted it out. He bit the carrot again, harder. The tooth stayed. He tried a drink of cold milk. Still there. Then he bit an apple slice. Crack! The tooth popped right out. "It came out because the apple is hard," Nathan said. "The carrot was too little. The apple was big and hard!"

Mom laugh... no, Mom and Dad both began to laugh. Mom held up her hand. "This is a sign," she said. "You are growing up, Nathan!" Nathan put the tooth in a small cup. He could not wait for the tooth fairy. He grinned his big new gap-tooth grin. "Look at me!" he said.

activity: Sophia is learning something new. What Sophia is learning: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour.
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Paint day at school! Sophia ran to the paint cups.

Teacher Mia held up a cup. "Red," said Sophia. "Blue. Yellow." She counted them: one, two, three. The three colours waited like sleepy little frogs.

"I want purple paint," said Sophia. "Where is purple?"

Teacher Mia smiled. "Look for it."

Sophia looked. No purple cup. Her friend Tomo was stirring his brush round and round. The red paint and the blue paint fell into one cup. Swirl, swirl, swirl.

"Look!" said Tomo. The cup held purple.

Sophia gasped. Her ear felt cool where a drop of paint had landed. She dipped her brush in red, then in blue. She stirred.

"Red and blue make purple," said Sophia. "They stay purple! Purple for me!"

She painted a big purple cat with green eyes. "Meow," said Sophia.

activity: Through what Claire sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Claire sat in her car seat. She was going to the farm with Dad. She hugged her white rabbit, Mr. Flop.

"Buckle in, Mr. Flop," said Claire. But Mr. Flop slid down. He fell onto the floor. His leg was stuck under the seat.

"Help!" said Claire. "Dad, can you help, please? Mr. Flop fell."

Dad reached back one hand. He pulled Mr. Flop up. He set the rabbit on Claire's lap.

"Thank you, Dad," said Claire. "You saved him."

Then the car went over a bump. Claire squeezed Mr. Flop too hard. Rip! His ear made a little hole.

"Oh no," said Claire. "I am so sorry, Mr. Flop. I did not mean it."

She held his ear together with her hand. She pretended her hand was magic tape. The ear stayed put.

At the farm, Mom looked at the hole. "I can sew it later," she said. "Would you like to hold him while we drive home?"

"Yes, please," said Claire.

The sheep said, "Baaa." Mr. Flop wiggled, like he was saying hello back.

activity: Through what Beau sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back.
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Beau sat on his bed with his library book. It was about a turtle who had a strong shell. Beau loved the turtle. He wanted to keep the book forever.

He hid the book under his pillow. "Now it is mine," he said. He patted the pillow. But then he heard the paper crinkle. He lifted the pillow and looked at the cover. The turtle looked sad on the page.

The next day, Mom drove Beau back to the library. Beau gave the book to the lady at the desk. He turned the pages from the front to the back. He pointed at the words. "This says turtle," he said. "Somebody can read it now."

A small girl took the book next. She hugged it tight. "Thank you," she whispered. Beau smiled and picked out a new book about fish. He held it the right way. Front cover first. Then he opened page one and began.

activity: Mia is making an art or craft project.
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Mia wanted to paint a big frog. She had red paint. She had blue paint. She had yellow paint too. But she did not have green.

The frog on her page waited. Mia looked and looked. No green paint anywhere.

Mama sat down next to her. "You have lots of colors," said Mama. Mia frowned at her pots.

Mia put a blob of yellow in her cup. Then she added a blob of blue. She took her brush and began to stir. Round and round went the brush. Slowly the yellow changed. Slowly the blue changed too. The cup turned green!

Mia dipped her brush. She painted the frog green from head to toes. "Look, Mama!" said Mia. "I made green!"

Outside, the rain began to fall. It made soft taps on the window. Mia painted rain too. She made green grass under the frog.

"Can I make more colors?" asked Mia.

"Yes," said Mama. She brought a clean cup.

Mia stirred red and yellow. It turned orange, bright as a wild tiger. She laughed and dipped her brush again.

activity: Through what Charlie sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Charlie was in the backyard with Dad. She wanted to find the pretty flower. "Where is it hiding?" she asked.

Charlie looked with her eyes. She saw grass and a big tree. Then she heard a buzz with her ears. A bee went by. The bee flew to the flower. "I see it!" said Charlie.

Charlie sniffed with her nose. The flower smelled sweet. But something else smelled bad. "Pee-yew! What is smelly?" she said. She followed her nose. It was an old shoe by the fence. Charlie touched the shoe with her fingers. It was wet and squishy. She did not touch it again.

"Can I taste a flower?" asked Charlie. Dad said no. "Flowers are for looking, not for eating." So Charlie just sniffed it. Her nose knew the sweet smell from the bad one.

"What should we do with the shoe?" asked Dad. "Draw it!" said Charlie. She got her crayons. She drew the shoe with a big stink line on top. Dad laughed. "Good picture," he said. Charlie sniffed the flower one more time.

activity: Through what Muhammad sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle.
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Muhammad sat at the little table in art class. He wanted to paint a house. But his paper looked wrong. His house had no windows and no door.

Teacher Amira gave him a bucket of brushes. "Pick a shape," she said. Muhammad picked the circle stamp. He dipped it in blue paint. He pressed it down. A round window appeared! "A circle makes a round window," he said.

He tried the square stamp. He pressed it hard. Now the house had a square window too. Then he stamped a rectangle. It made a long red door. "Hello, door!" he said, and laughed.

He still needed a roof. He looked in the bucket. He found the triangle stamp. He dipped it in sticky brown paint. He sniffed it. "Yuck, this paint is stinky!" he said. Teacher Amira laughed. "That one is old," she said. She brought fresh paint. Muhammad stamped one triangle on top. The house was done. He held it up high. "Look! My house can live on the wall now!"

activity: Through what Mason sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Mason stood by the snack table at school. Miss Kim had a big surprise. It was a guessing game, and Mason wanted to win.

"Close your eyes," said Miss Kim. "No peeking!"

First there was a sound. Crunch, crunch. Mason used his ears to hear it. "Crackers!" he said.

Next came a smell. Mason used his nose. "Banana!" he said. He was right again.

Then something touched his hand, and his hand felt it. "A short spoon!" he laughed. Then a cold apple touched his cheek. His cheek felt the cold.

Last was a taste on his tongue. Sweet and juicy. "Orange!" said Mason. "Yes!" said Miss Kim, and she gave him a big sticker.

"My eyes missed everything," said Mason. "My ears, my nose, my tongue and my hands did it all!" He put the sticker on his shirt and skipped to the computer corner.

activity: Through what Charlotte sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods.
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Charlotte went to the park with her teddy bear. She wanted to build a pretend picnic. First she found a flat rock for a table. Then she set out her toys. The teddy sat on one side. Her toy bunny sat on the other side.

Now she needed pretend food. She picked a leaf. "This is a big green cookie," she said. She picked a little stick. "This is a skinny banana." She put them on the rock. Her teddy and bunny were ready to eat.

Then a duck walked over. The duck looked at the leaf. The duck took the leaf and ate it! Charlotte clapped. More birds came hopping. "You are animals, not toys," she told them. "But you can come too." The duck quacked and took the skinny banana too.

activity: Charles is searching for a lost favorite toy.
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Charles lost his small blue bunny. He looked under the table. Bunny was not there. He looked in the toy box. Bunny was not there either.

His teacher Ms. Kim knelt down. "Where did you play with bunny today?" Charles thought hard. "At the milk table," he said. "I had my cup of milk there." He ran to the little chairs. He got down on his knees. He peeked under his own seat.

There was bunny, soft and warm, resting by the wall. Charles hugged him tight. "You were where I left you," he said. "I played there, so you stayed there." He smiled a big smile. Then he and bunny went to sit with the other young children for story time. "More milk?" asked Ms. Kim kindly. Charles nodded and held bunny on his lap.

activity: Through what Hazel sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Hazel sat in her car seat. Today they were going to Grandma's lake house. Yesterday they had packed a bag. Tomorrow they would go out on Grandma's boat.

"Are we there yet?" Hazel asked.

"Not yet," said Daddy. "We will get there later. Look out the window now."

Hazel looked. The sun was up now. Soon the sun went down. The sky turned pink. Then it turned dark.

"Look, the moon," said Mommy. "The sun went away. Now the moon is here."

Hazel watched the moon follow the car. It looked big and fuzzy behind a cloud. Later, the moon went away too. Then Hazel saw water. And a small boat. And Grandma, waving by the door.

"Grandma!" Hazel called. "I saw the sun go down!"

Grandma opened the car door and hugged her tight.
